section.title: Walking by the Spirit
section.sectionRationale: Paul answers how the free person actually lives a holy life, not by law but by the Spirit. He sets the works of the flesh against the fruit of the Spirit, showing two opposed powers at war within. Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh, and since they live by the Spirit they are to keep in step with the Spirit. Holiness is the harvest of walking with the Spirit, not the achievement of law keeping.
section.thesis: The believer walks in holiness not by law but by the Spirit, in whom the flesh and the Spirit war against each other; the works of the flesh are obvious and exclude from the kingdom, but the fruit of the Spirit grows in those who belong to Christ and have crucified the flesh, so they must keep in step with the Spirit.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the command to walk by the Spirit and the war between flesh and Spirit; the works of the flesh contrasted with the fruit of the Spirit; and the crucified flesh and the call to keep in step with the Spirit.

units.label: The war between flesh and Spirit
units.note: walk by the Spirit and you will not gratify the flesh

verses.text: So I say, walk by the {{pneuma|Spirit}}, and you will not gratify the desires of the {{sarx|flesh}}.
For the flesh craves what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh. They are opposed to each other, so that you do not do what you want.
But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.

units.label: Works of the flesh, fruit of the Spirit
units.note: two harvests set side by side

verses.text: The acts of the flesh are obvious: sexual immorality, impurity, and debauchery;
idolatry and sorcery; hatred, discord, jealousy, and rage; rivalries, divisions, factions,
and envy; drunkenness, orgies, and the like. I warn you, as I did before, that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.
But the {{karpos|fruit}} of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness,
gentleness, and {{egkrateia|self-control}}. Against such things there is no law.

units.label: Crucified flesh, keeping in step
units.note: live by the Spirit, walk by the Spirit

verses.text: Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.
Since we live by the Spirit, let us walk in step with the Spirit.
Let us not become conceited, provoking and envying one another.

pneuma.gloss: Spirit, the Holy Spirit, the indwelling power of God in the believer. The whole passage answers how to live a holy life: by walking in the Spirit, being led by the Spirit, and keeping in step with the Spirit. Holiness is not self generated law keeping but the fruit the Spirit produces in those He indwells, so the Christian life is lived from the Spirit's power, not the flesh's effort.

sarx.gloss: Flesh, here not the physical body but the fallen human nature in rebellion against God, the self ruled by sinful desire. The flesh wars against the Spirit and produces its obvious works. Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh, yet its desires still press, so the believer must keep walking by the Spirit rather than gratifying the flesh.

karpos.gloss: Fruit, the natural produce of a living plant. Paul calls the Spirit's work fruit, not works, because it grows organically from the Spirit's life within rather than being manufactured by effort. Notice it is singular, one fruit with many facets, love, joy, peace, and the rest, a single ripening character that the Spirit produces in the believer.

egkrateia.gloss: Self-control, mastery over one's desires and impulses. It stands last in the list of the Spirit's fruit, showing that true self control is itself a gift of the Spirit, not merely willpower. The Spirit who frees us from the law also produces the disciplined, ordered life that no law could compel, for against such things there is no law.

basic.context: Having freed the Galatians from the law, Paul answers the obvious question: how then do we live holy lives? His answer is the Spirit. Inside every believer the flesh and the Spirit are at war. If you walk by the Spirit, you will not carry out the flesh's desires. The flesh produces ugly, obvious works; the Spirit produces a beautiful, ripening character. Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh, so they should keep in step with the Spirit.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the practical answer to the whole letter: freedom from law does not mean freedom to sin, because the Spirit produces holiness. Read the two lists as two harvests from two different roots, and notice that the answer to sin is not more law but more of the Spirit.
basic.originalLanguages: The command is to walk by the pneuma, the Spirit, and not gratify the sarx, the flesh, the fallen self. The Spirit produces karpos, fruit, a single ripening character, and it ends with egkrateia, self-control, itself a gift of the Spirit rather than mere willpower.
basic.typology: Crucifying the flesh continues the theme of being crucified with Christ from 2:20: the believer's union with the crucified Lord means death to the old self. The fruit of the Spirit is the restored image of God in humanity, the character of Christ formed in His people by the Spirit.
basic.christ: Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh. The fruit of the Spirit is nothing less than the character of Christ reproduced in the believer, love, joy, peace, and the rest. The Spirit at work is the Spirit of Christ, forming the likeness of Jesus in those who are His.
basic.god: God gives the Spirit who wages war against the flesh and produces holiness. The kingdom of God is the inheritance from which the works of the flesh exclude, so God is both the giver of the Spirit and the King whose kingdom is at stake. He makes His people holy by His own indwelling power.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 8 says those led by the Spirit put to death the deeds of the body. John 15 speaks of abiding in Christ to bear much fruit. Ephesians 5 contrasts the works of darkness with the fruit of light.
basic.oneStory: The gospel does not stop at forgiveness; it makes new people. The Spirit poured out in the last days, promised by the prophets, produces in believers the character God always intended, undoing the works of the flesh and forming the likeness of Christ, a preview of the holiness of the new creation.

context.literary:
The section stands in the middle of Paul's practical turn, between the warning about biting and devouring in 5:15 and the picture of a community restoring its fallen in 6:1. Its frame is a pair of commands about walking. In verse 16 Paul says to walk by the Spirit, and in verse 25 he says to keep in step with the Spirit. Everything between those two verses is the argument that makes those commands possible: the war inside the believer, the two harvests, and the death of the old self.

The central contrast is built on a grammatical difference that is easy to miss. The deeds of the flesh are 'works,' plural, a pile of separate acts, while the Spirit's contribution is 'fruit,' singular, one growth with many aspects. The list of nine in verses 22 and 23 is therefore not a menu from which a believer chooses but a single character seen from several sides. The works are things people do, the fruit is something that grows in people, and Paul does not say the Spirit's fruit comes by effort.

The two lists are also arranged with care. The works of the flesh fall into groups: sexual sins, sins of false worship, sins of social breakdown, and sins of excess. The middle group is the longest and the most telling for this letter, since it names hatred, discord, jealousy, rage, rivalries, divisions, factions and envy, exactly the symptoms of a community that is biting and devouring, 5:15. The fruit list begins with love, which Paul has just called the fulfilment of the law, and ends with self-control, and most of it concerns relationships.

Verse 23 ends the lists with a dry legal remark, 'Against such things there is no law,' which returns to the argument of the letter: no one writes statutes against love. Verses 24 to 26 then bring the whole to rest with a statement about belonging, an instruction, and a warning against the very pride and envy that opened the list of works.
context.historical:
Galatia was a place where the temptation to live by rules was not only religious but cultural. Greco-Roman moral teachers commonly offered lists of vices and virtues, and the Galatians would have recognised the form Paul uses. The lists of Paul are not copies of those lists; the virtues he names are not the classical ones, and most of them concern a person's way of treating others. Courage, prudence and the like are missing, while patience, kindness and gentleness stand in the front.

The works of the flesh would also have rung true to the daily life of a Gentile convert. Idolatry and sorcery belonged to the temples and trades of the cities, and the drunken feasts that Paul names were part of public religious life. Paul had warned them before, he says in verse 21, and his readers knew they were being asked to leave that world.

The problem he faced in Galatia was that two different groups were pulling the church apart. The agitators wanted to bring law in, and some who rejected the law may have been tempted to treat freedom as permission. Paul's answer works against both. The church could not be held together by rules about circumcision and calendar, and it could not be held together by a licence that let every desire have its way.

The idea of the Spirit as the mark of God's people also had a long background. The prophets had promised that God would put His Spirit within His people, Ezekiel 36:26-27, and that in the last days He would pour the Spirit on all, Joel 2:28-29. The Galatians had received the Spirit when they believed, Galatians 3:2-5, and Paul tells them that this gift, not a legal code, is how the promised new life is realised.
context.canonical:
The Old Testament never treats holiness as a matter of law alone. Moses wished that all the Lord's people were prophets, Numbers 11:29, and the later prophets look ahead to a day when the law would be written on the heart and the Spirit would move people to walk in God's ways. Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:27 stand behind Paul's argument that the Spirit does what the law could never do.

The image of fruit is at home in the wisdom and prophetic tradition. Psalm 1 pictures the righteous as a tree that yields its fruit in season, and Jesus later says that a tree is known by its fruit, Matthew 7:16-20. In John 15:1-8 He says that His disciples bear much fruit by remaining in Him, and apart from Him they can do nothing. Paul's picture is the same: the believer bears fruit because of union with Christ through the Spirit.

The contrast between flesh and Spirit is developed at length in Romans 8:5-14, where Paul says that those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the flesh, and that all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. Romans 7 shows the struggle from the standpoint of a person under law, and Romans 8 shows the way out. Galatians 5 is the shorter, sharper version of the same teaching.

Other lists in the New Testament run parallel. Colossians 3:5-17 asks believers to put to death what is earthly and to put on compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience, and Ephesians 5:9 speaks of 'the fruit of the light.' The warning that those who live in such ways will not inherit the kingdom is repeated in 1 Corinthians 6:9-10 and Ephesians 5:5, and 2 Peter 1:5-8 sets out a similar growth of character.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wrote to keep the Galatians from two disasters at once. If the law was not going to make them holy, would anything? He answered that the Spirit would, and that the Spirit would do it more deeply than any code. He wanted them to see that their situation was not hopeless without law, because God had given them a power greater than the flesh.

He also wanted them to take the fight seriously. Verse 17 is not a comfortable verse. It tells them that two forces are active inside them, and that the resulting struggle is real. A Galatian who thought that freedom meant the end of struggle would be disappointed; Paul wants them to expect the war and to know how it is won, by walking by the Spirit, not by trying harder at the law.

The lists are meant to function as a mirror. The works of the flesh are 'obvious,' and Paul expects the readers to see themselves and their communities in the second half of the list. The fruit is meant to become the goal they pray for and the standard by which they judge their common life. Most pointedly, the final warning in verse 26 about conceit, provoking and envy is aimed at the very factional spirit that was tearing the churches apart.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The lists are descriptions with an edge. The works of the flesh are what the flesh produces, and the fruit of the Spirit is what the Spirit produces. Neither list is a checklist of rules to be ticked off, and the passage should not be read as a set of nine tasks. The fruit is not a to-do list but a description of what God is growing, and the believer's part is to walk by the Spirit and to keep in step.

It is not a complete catalogue either. Paul says 'and the like' at the end of the works of the flesh, and 'against such things' after the fruit, which suggests he is giving samples. The point of the lists is the direction of life, not a full inventory of every sin and every virtue.

The commands are prescriptive: walk, keep in step, crucify, and do not become conceited. The warning in verse 21 is also a serious statement about those whose lives are characterised by the flesh. What it does not do is turn every lapse into a sign of damnation, as the debate on verse 21 shows. Believers are told to put the flesh to death with the same breath that says it has already been crucified. That tension is intentional, and it describes the Christian life between the first coming of Christ and the second.

debates.question: Does the warning of verse 21 threaten believers with loss of the kingdom?

views.label: A description of those whose lives are marked by the flesh
views.case: The present participle, 'those who practice such things,' points to a settled pattern of life, not an isolated fall. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 6:11 that some of the Corinthians were once such people but had been washed and sanctified. On this view the verse marks the difference between the unregenerate and the Spirit-led, and believers are assured of perseverance.

views.label: A real warning to believers
views.case: Paul says 'I warn you, as I did before,' and addresses it to a church in danger. Many hold that the warnings of the New Testament are the means God uses to keep His people persevering, and that they should be taken as written. A believer who ignores them is in genuine danger.

views.label: A test of profession
views.case: Some read it as a test of whether faith is real: genuine faith produces the fruit of the Spirit, and a life that bears only the works of the flesh calls the profession into question. This is close to Jesus' teaching that a tree is known by its fruit, Matthew 7:16-20.

debates.bearing: On all three readings the warning is meant to be heard and obeyed, and the cure is the same: walk by the Spirit. No view should be held in such a way that the warning stops working.

debates.question: What does 'so that you do not do what you want' in verse 17 mean?

views.label: The flesh frustrates the believer's good intentions
views.case: On this reading, the believer wants to do good but the flesh pulls the other way, as in Romans 7:15-20. The struggle is real and continues through life.

views.label: The Spirit frustrates the flesh's evil intentions
views.case: Others read it the other way: the Spirit prevents the believer from doing whatever the flesh wants, so that sin does not have free rein. This fits verses 16 and 18, where the Spirit leads and the flesh is not gratified.

views.label: Both at once
views.case: A third view holds that Paul states the stalemate of two forces, and that the following verses show the way out. Neither the flesh nor the Spirit gets its way without a contest, and the believer's walk by the Spirit tips the balance.

debates.bearing: The Greek can bear more than one sense, and the surrounding verses guard against despair. Whatever the exact force, Paul's point is that the believer is no longer simply the flesh's captive, since the Spirit is on the believer's side.

study.originalLanguages:
The command of verse 16 is a present imperative, 'keep walking,' from a verb that means to walk about and, in Paul's vocabulary, to conduct one's life. The promise that follows uses the strongest form of Greek negation, a double negative that can be rendered 'you will certainly not carry out' the desires of the flesh. The verb is the ordinary word for finishing or bringing something to completion, so that the flesh has desires but never gets them carried through to completion for those who walk by the Spirit.

The word 'flesh' keeps recurring from verse 13 to verse 24, and in this passage it does not mean the body as such. It is the whole self as it stands apart from God, with its own appetites and ambitions. That explains why the works of the flesh include things like jealousy, rivalry and factions that have nothing to do with bodily appetite. The 'desires' of the flesh in verse 16 are the same word in verse 24 joined with 'passions,' and in both verses they belong to the self that has been put to death in Christ.

In verse 18 'led' is a present passive, 'if you are being led,' picturing the Spirit as the leader and the believer as the one led. Romans 8:14 uses the same form. The person who is led by the Spirit is not under the law, which is not a statement that the law is evil but that its role as the guard and supervisor has been fulfilled, as Galatians 3:23-25 has said.

In the list of the works of the flesh, 'sorcery' translates a word that gives us pharmacy, and it refers to the use of drugs and potions in magic, a practice bound up with idolatry. 'Rivalries' names a spirit of contention, and 'factions' is the word from which we get 'heresy,' here meaning a party spirit that splits a community. The word for drunkenness and 'orgies' names the drinking parties and riotous revels common in ancient cities.

The Greek of verse 22 is in the singular: 'the fruit of the Spirit is.' The word for 'kindness' and the word for 'goodness' are distinct, and the word 'faithfulness' can also be translated 'faith,' though in this list of qualities of character it is naturally taken as dependability. 'Gentleness' is the quality seen in 6:1. The last word, 'self-control,' is formed from a root that means holding oneself, and its place at the end is striking, since it is the one virtue a person might think of as the work of the will.

Verse 25 uses a different verb for walking than verse 16. It is the word for keeping in line, as soldiers keep rank, and it is related to the word Paul used in 4:25 for Hagar 'corresponding to' the present Jerusalem. The same family of words that described the slave column now describes the Spirit's column. In verse 26 'conceited' is made from the words for empty and glory, so those who are conceited are those who pursue empty glory.

typology.type: The crucified flesh and the cross of Christ
typology.fulfillment: Paul says that those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh. The picture comes from the cross of Jesus and from Paul's own testimony in Galatians 2:20, 'I have been crucified with Christ.' In Christ's death the old self was nailed up, Romans 6:6, and believers share that death by faith. The correspondence is complete in the sense that the fate of the old self is settled, and yet it is lived out day by day, as Colossians 3:5 says. The type falls short in that Christ's death was sufficient, while the believer's putting to death of sin continues throughout life.

typology.type: The fruit of the Spirit and the image of God
typology.fulfillment: Humanity was made in God's image, Genesis 1:27, and the image was marred in the fall. The fruit of the Spirit is the likeness of God restored, and most of the nine qualities are ones Scripture ascribes to God Himself, Exodus 34:6. In Christ the image is seen perfectly, Colossians 1:15, and believers are being renewed in the likeness of their Creator, Colossians 3:10. The type is not yet complete, for we shall be fully like Him only when we see Him, 1 John 3:2.

Israel was led through the wilderness by a pillar of cloud and fire, Exodus 13:21, and the psalmist asks that God's good Spirit lead him on level ground, Psalm 143:10. Paul says that those who are led by the Spirit are God's sons, Romans 8:14. The guidance of the Spirit is more intimate than the pillar, since He dwells within, and the destination is not a land but conformity to Christ. The type falls short in that the pillar went before the people and was seen by all, whereas the Spirit leads from inside the believer.

The Old Testament often presents two paths, as in Deuteronomy 30:15-19 and Psalm 1, where life and death, blessing and curse, are set before the people. Paul's two lists belong to that tradition. In Christ the choice is not simply put before us, but resolved: Christ has borne the curse and given the Spirit, so that the path of life can actually be walked, Galatians 3:13-14. The type falls short in that the old choice was put to a people who could not by themselves choose well.

study.christ:
The passage speaks of Christ in three ways. First, believers belong to Him. 'Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh,' verse 24, so that identity with Christ is the ground of everything else in the passage. They do not crucify the flesh in order to belong to Him; they do it because they belong. The sequence matches Galatians 2:20 and Romans 6:11: union with Christ in His death and life comes first, and the fight against sin is its consequence.

Second, the fruit is the character of Christ. Each of the nine qualities can be read in the Gospels as a description of Jesus: His love, His joy, the peace He left His disciples, His patience with the slow, the kindness shown to sinners, His goodness, His faithfulness to the Father, His gentleness with the weary, and His self-control in the wilderness and before Pilate. When the Spirit produces this fruit, He is forming Christ in His people, which is exactly what Paul prays for in Galatians 4:19. The Spirit is called the Spirit of Christ in Romans 8:9, and He does not work apart from Him.

Third, the passage points to the cross as the place where the war was decided. Paul does not say that the flesh will be crucified, as though it were a future task, but that it has been. The flesh and its passions were dealt with in Christ's death. That does not end the struggle, but it changes it from a campaign for survival into a mop-up of an enemy whose power was broken. Paul says in Galatians 6:14 that through the cross the world has been crucified to him and he to the world.

The warnings of verses 19 to 21 also take on weight in the light of the cross. Christ bore the penalty of such deeds, and for believers to take them up again is to treat lightly the cost of their freedom. Paul links the two in 1 Corinthians 6:11, where the washed, sanctified and justified believers are called to live out what has been done for them.

We should not push the passage beyond what it says. It does not make Christ the fruit itself, nor does it suggest that each quality corresponds to a particular moment in the Gospels. The link rests on the broad pattern of the New Testament, that the Spirit conforms believers to the likeness of the Son, Romans 8:29 and 2 Corinthians 3:18.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who gives Himself. The Spirit is not an impersonal force but the One who leads, who has desires that oppose the flesh, who produces fruit, and with whom believers keep in step. Paul speaks of the Spirit in personal terms throughout. The Spirit is also the Spirit of the Son sent into believers' hearts, Galatians 4:6, so the doctrine of God in this passage is Trinitarian in its working: the Father who has adopted, the Son in whom believers have died to the flesh, and the Spirit who enables a new life.

God is holy, and His holiness is not satisfied with a pardon that leaves the person unchanged. The kingdom He rules is not open to those whose lives are given over to the works of the flesh, and Paul will not soften that. The same holy God, however, does not leave His people to produce their own holiness. He supplies what He commands. The fruit of the Spirit is a way of saying that holiness is God's own work in His people, as Philippians 2:13 says, God is at work in His people both to will and to act.

He is patient and kind, and the fruit that the Spirit bears includes both qualities. The fruit list is in large part a portrait of God's own character, so that when His people show patience, kindness and gentleness they are showing what He is like. Exodus 34:6 describes the Lord as compassionate, gracious, slow to anger and abounding in love and faithfulness, and several of those qualities reappear in Paul's list.

He is a God who honours His law while moving beyond it. 'Against such things there is no law' does not mean the law was wrong, but that the aim of the law is reached in a life of love. The law's demands are not abolished but fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit, Romans 8:4.

For worship, the passage teaches dependence. The believer cannot manufacture fruit, only abide, walk and keep in step. It teaches thanksgiving, for every good quality in a believer's life is a gift. And it teaches hope, since the God who began the work is the God who will carry it to completion, Philippians 1:6.

crossReferences.note: The fullest parallel. Those who live according to the flesh set their minds on it, those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the Spirit, and by the Spirit they put to death the deeds of the body. All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.

The same struggle seen from the other side. The person under law wants to do good but cannot carry it out, and cries out for rescue. Galatians 5:17 compresses this experience, and Romans 8 gives the answer that Galatians 5:16 gives in a line.

The earlier statement of crucifixion with Christ. 'I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me.' Galatians 5:24 describes what that same truth means for the whole company of believers, and it shows that the crucifixion of the flesh rests on union with Christ.

A parallel pair of lists. Believers are told to put to death what is earthly, such as sexual immorality, impurity, evil desire and greed, and to put on compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience. It shows that the two lists were a regular part of Paul's teaching.

Jesus says that those who remain in Him bear much fruit, and that apart from Him they can do nothing. The picture of fruit growing from a living connection explains why Paul says 'fruit' and not 'work,' and why the believer must keep in step with the Spirit.

A tree is known by its fruit. Grapes do not come from thornbushes, and a good tree cannot bear bad fruit. Paul's contrast between works and fruit follows the same logic, that a life reveals its source.

God promises to give a new heart and to put His Spirit within His people and cause them to walk in His statutes. This is the Old Testament promise behind Galatians 5, and it shows that walking by the Spirit is the fulfilment of what the prophets foretold.

A parallel list of those who will not inherit the kingdom, followed by the word that some of the believers had been such people but were washed, sanctified and justified. It shows how the warning and the assurance belong together in Paul's teaching.

Paul's question about whether the Galatians received the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith. The Spirit was the starting point of their Christian life, and Paul asks whether they now think they can finish by the flesh.

God predestined His people to be conformed to the image of His Son. The fruit of the Spirit is the daily outworking of this purpose, so that the character of Christ is formed in those who belong to Him.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture begins with people made to bear God's image and walk with Him in the garden, and it ends with a city in which He walks among His people. The long middle of the story is the account of why that walk broke down and how it is restored. In Eden the desires of the heart pulled against God's word, and the Old Testament shows how a whole nation with the law in their hands still could not keep walking with Him.

The prophets answered with a promise rather than a rule. God would give His people a new heart and put His Spirit within them, so that they would walk in His ways, Ezekiel 36:26-27. Joel looked to a day when the Spirit would be poured out on all flesh. Galatians 5 is the announcement that the day has come. The Spirit given at Pentecost and given to the Galatians when they believed is the beginning of that promised life, and the fruit is the harvest of it.

The war in verse 17 is the war of the in-between time. The old age has not yet passed, and the flesh is still active, but the new age has begun, and the Spirit is the first instalment of what is to come, Romans 8:23. Believers live in the overlap, with the verdict on the flesh already given at the cross and the full freedom of the new creation still to be revealed.

The end of the story is the end of the war. The works of the flesh will have no place in the city, Revelation 22:15, and the tree of life will grow beside the river, with leaves for the healing of the nations, Revelation 22:2. The fruit that the Spirit now begins to bear in imperfect form will be complete, and the character of Christ will be fully formed in His people, 1 John 3:2. The church that the Galatians were beginning to tear apart by rivalry will at last be a community of love, and its gentleness, its joy and its peace will fill the new creation.

sermon.title: How to Change (Galatians 5:16 to 18, 22 to 25)
sermon.why: Keller expounds how real change comes through the fruit of the Spirit rather than mere willpower or law keeping, showing how walking by the Spirit produces the character of Christ in the believer.

quiz.q: How does Paul say we overcome the desires of the flesh?

options.text: By walking by the Spirit.
options.note: Verse 16 gives the Spirit, not the law, as the answer.

options.text: By trying harder to keep the law.
options.note: The answer to the flesh is the Spirit, not renewed law keeping.

options.text: By avoiding all contact with the world.
options.note: The battle is won by walking in the Spirit, not mere withdrawal.

options.text: By ignoring the flesh and hoping it fades.
options.note: Paul commands active walking by the Spirit, not passivity.

quiz.q: What is the relationship between the flesh and the Spirit?

options.text: They are opposed to each other, at war within the believer.
options.note: Verse 17 describes the ongoing conflict.

options.text: They work together in harmony.
options.note: They are opposed, not harmonious.

options.text: The flesh has already been completely removed.
options.note: The flesh is crucified yet its desires still press, so the war continues.

options.text: The Spirit rarely acts in a believer.
options.note: The Spirit actively wars against the flesh and produces fruit.

quiz.q: Why does Paul call the Spirit's produce fruit rather than works?

options.text: Because it grows organically from the Spirit's life within, not manufactured by effort.
options.note: The singular fruit grows from the Spirit, unlike self made works.

options.text: Because it is optional for believers.
options.note: It is the natural mark of the Spirit's presence, not optional.

options.text: Because it can be produced by willpower alone.
options.note: The point is that it is the Spirit's produce, not mere willpower.

options.text: Because it has nothing to do with character.
options.note: The fruit is precisely Christlike character formed by the Spirit.

quiz.q: What is true of those who belong to Christ Jesus?

options.text: They have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.
options.note: Verse 24 describes their decisive break with the flesh.

options.text: They no longer experience any temptation.
options.note: The flesh is crucified, yet its desires still war, so temptation remains.

options.text: They are free to indulge the flesh.
options.note: Belonging to Christ means crucifying the flesh, not indulging it.

options.text: They rely on the law for holiness.
options.note: Holiness comes by the Spirit, not the law.

quiz.q: What does verse 25 call believers to do?

options.text: Since we live by the Spirit, to keep in step with the Spirit.
options.note: Life in the Spirit is to be matched by walking in the Spirit.

options.text: To relax, since the Spirit does everything without us.
options.note: Keeping in step is active, not passive.

options.text: To return to the law for daily guidance.
options.note: The call is to walk by the Spirit, not the law.

options.text: To compete with one another for status.
options.note: Verse 26 warns against conceit and provoking one another.

questions: Paul says the answer to the flesh is the Spirit, not the law. When you struggle with sin, do you reach first for willpower and rules, or for dependence on the Spirit?
The fruit of the Spirit is a single, ripening character. Which facet of that fruit is the Spirit most clearly growing in you right now, and which is least developed?
Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh. What passion or desire do you need to treat as crucified rather than negotiated with?
Keeping in step with the Spirit is active, daily dependence. What would it look like practically to walk with the Spirit through tomorrow?
The works of the flesh include rivalries, divisions, and envy. How do these show up in your relationships, and how does the Spirit offer a different way?

translationNotes.note: Flesh renders sarx, here the fallen human nature in rebellion against God, not the physical body; the contrast is with the Spirit, not with material existence.
Fruit is singular in the Greek, one fruit with many facets, in deliberate contrast to the plural works of the flesh; the Spirit produces a unified character.
Against such things there is no law means the Spirit's fruit needs no law to restrain it and no law can produce it; it fulfills what the law aimed at.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Galatians 5:16-26. Sermon verified this session from the Gospel in Life series Galatians: New Freedom, New Family by Tim Keller.
